- 15.09.2024 re-appointment: not valid - she is within the 5-year bar; PQR filing its FS on 08.05.2024 does not remove the disqualification.

questions.ask: As management, show from the summary financial statements that management is efficient.
questions.clue: 'how will you indicate the efficiency of the management... summary of financial statements'

questions.answer:
Measure: Economic Value Added - profit left after charging the cost of ALL capital (debt and equity).

Working (Rs lakh):
Tax rate u/s 115BAB = 15% + SC 10% + HEC 4% = 17.16%
EBIT 724.29 less tax @17.16% (124.29) = 600.00
Add: bad-debt provision (non-cash) = 50.00
NOPAT = 650.00

Total assets 2,500 less non-interest-bearing liabilities 400 = capital employed 2,100
Add: provision 50 -> invested capital 2,150

WACC = 1,800/2,100 x 9% + 300/2,100 x 15% x (1 - 0.1716) = 7.71% + 1.78% = 9.49%
Capital charge = 2,150 x 9.49% = 204.04
EVA = 650.00 - 204.04 = 445.96

Interpretation:
- EVA is large and positive: return on invested capital about 30% against a 9.49% cost of capital.
- Costs are under control (EBIT margin about 29%), debt is a small, cheap part of capital (post-tax 12.4%), and the concessional 115BAB rate lifts post-tax returns.
- Conclusion: management's decisions have created shareholder value; management is efficient.

(If NOPAT is built from the given EBT of 600: NOPAT 629.88, EVA 425.84 - ICAI accepts this too.)

(Rs lakh) | Goodwill | Other assets | Total

questions.subject: Costing
questions.chapter: SCMPE - Supply Chain Management (upstream and downstream)
questions.topic: Upstream (inbound) and downstream (outbound) supply chain strategies
questions.ask: Discuss how EVML improved its inbound and outbound supply chain to cut costs, cut inventory and raise customer satisfaction.
questions.clue: 'It was decided to revamp its inbound and outbound supply chain'
think: 'Inbound and outbound supply chain' = upstream and downstream SCM - the SM headings ARE the answer structure

SCMPE -> supply chain management -> upstream: supplier relationship, number of suppliers, cost-quality-speed, make or buy, IT; downstream: relationship marketing, CRM, customer selection-acquisition-retention-extension, IT, brand
Under each heading put 1-2 case facts with figures (examiners marked down generic text and missing headings)
Close with the result: inventory down 75%, net saving Rs 18.30 crore, profit up in 2023-24

look_up.where: ICAI SCMPE - Supply Chain Management

questions.solve: Map each case paragraph to an SM heading. Inbound: JIT + pull; value engineering; supplier partnership with cost-sharing and technical help; Pareto (25% of suppliers = 80% of business) and cut from 1,500 to 800 via tiering/system buying; supplier warehouses 35-40 minutes away; ABC classification with delivery norms; JIT cards by email; single-window vendor system; maximum bought-out parts with global sourcing; RFID, GPS, EDI, bar codes. Outbound: regional distribution centres, product-wise delivery schedules, 3S dealerships, 24x7 outlets and mobile vans, dealer training twice a year, CRM forecasting, automated feedback on three service targets. Result: inventory 240 -> 60 crore, net saving 18.30 crore.
questions.answer:
Problem: a 14.29% revenue fall left inventories piling up; EVML re-geared ordering, handling, procurement and inventory control.

A. Inbound (upstream) supply chain
1. Supplier relationship - suppliers treated as partners in progress: technical help to meet quality and delivery; value-engineering savings shared with them.
2. Number of suppliers - 18,000+ parts mapped to supplier part numbers; Pareto showed 25% of 1,500 suppliers gave 80% of business and 60% gave 5%; base cut to 800 through tiering and system buying (deal only with tier-1, backed by tier-2 and tier-3).
3. Cost, quality and speed - value engineering to substitute costly materials and methods; JIT for high-value/low-volume items and low logistics cost for low-value/high-volume items; push replaced by pull; local suppliers' warehouses 35-40 minutes from the plants; ABC classification of parts and suppliers with separate delivery norms; JIT cards by email so parts go straight to the assembly line.
4. Make or buy - maximise bought-out parts, indigenous and imported; global sourcing on quality, price and delivery.
5. Information technology - single-window vendor management system (drawings, prices, quality issues); RFID, GPS tracking, EDI and bar coding.

B. Outbound (downstream) supply chain
1. Distribution - regional distribution centres at strategic points; separate delivery schedules for each product.
2. Relationship marketing - new 3S (Sales, Services, Spares) dealerships, 24x7 outlets and mobile service vans; dealer training twice a year (customer and dealer markets of the six markets model).
3. CRM - customer inputs used to track trends and forecast demand; automated post-delivery feedback set three service targets: order-to-delivery time, reliability of deliveries, order-status information.
4. Customer selection, acquisition, retention and extension - 1-year assurance warranty in the price, optional extended warranty (Rs 15,000), and the Board's resolve to fix technical errors even after warranty.
5. IT and brand - tracking, EDI and automated feedback in the dealer network; a reliable, service-led brand.

C. Result
Average inventory down 75% (Rs 240 crore to Rs 60 crore); net annual saving Rs 18.30 crore after JIT costs; faster delivery to customers and a significant rise in 2023-24 profit.

questions.trap: Writing generic supply-chain theory without inbound/outbound headings and case figures - examiners marked this below average for exactly that.

EUR loan: interest = 5,00,000 x 4.25% x 90/360 = 5,312.50 -> repay EUR 5,05,312.50. Forward Rs/EUR ask = 90.35 + 0.25 = 90.60. Outflow = 5,05,312.50 x 90.60 = Rs 4,57,81,312.50.

1. Euro loan
Principal EUR 5,00,000 + interest @4.25% x 90/360 = EUR 5,312.50 -> repay EUR 5,05,312.50
90-day forward Rs/EUR (ask) = 90.35 + 0.25 = 90.60
Rupee outflow = 5,05,312.50 x 90.60 = Rs 4,57,81,312.50

Primary adjustment: Rs 1.20 crore excess interest (3% on USD 45 lakh) added for AY 2023-24 and accepted by EVML.

Secondary adjustment u/s 92CE applies because:
(i) EVML has accepted the AO's primary adjustment;
(ii) it relates to AY 2023-24 (AY 2017-18 onwards); and
(iii) it exceeds Rs 1 crore.

Consequences:
1. EVML must repatriate the excess money of Rs 1.20 crore from its AE to India within 90 days of the AO's order (received 30.01.2025).

questions.topic: E-way bill for movement other than supply; retention 72 months or 1 year after appeal
questions.ask: Is an e-way bill needed for Rs 3 lakh of warranty replacement parts sent from Delhi to Mumbai? Till when must FY 2018-19 records be kept, with an appeal pending?
questions.clue: 'since the movement of goods is caused due to reasons other than supply'
think: Management's own words 'reasons other than supply' are the trap - rule 138(1) covers that too
IDT SM -> E-way Bill (rule 138) and Accounts and Records (s.36 retention)
Consignment Rs 3 lakh > Rs 50,000, inter-State -> e-way bill required (goods move on a delivery challan, no invoice)
Retention: 72 months from the due date of the FY 2018-19 annual return (31.12.2019 -> 31.12.2025; extended 31.12.2020 -> 31.12.2026) or 1 year after the appeal is disposed of, whichever is later

look_up.where: ICAI SM IDT - E-way Bill; Accounts and Records

questions.solve: Rule 138(1): an e-way bill must be generated before moving goods of consignment value above Rs 50,000 (i) in relation to a supply, (ii) for reasons other than supply, or (iii) due to inward supply from an unregistered person. Free warranty replacement is not a supply, but the movement is for reasons other than supply and the value is Rs 3 lakh -> e-way bill mandatory; goods move under a delivery challan. s.36: keep books till 72 months from the due date of the annual return for the year; a party to an appeal keeps records on its subject matter till 1 year after final disposal, or the 72 months, whichever is later. FY 2018-19 annual return due 31.12.2019 (extended to 31.12.2020) -> 31.12.2025 (or 31.12.2026).
questions.answer:
E-way bill:
- Replacement of parts under warranty without consideration is not a supply.
- But rule 138(1) of the CGST Rules requires an e-way bill for movement of goods of consignment value above Rs 50,000 even for reasons other than supply.
- Value Rs 3,00,000 > Rs 50,000 (inter-State, Delhi to Mumbai) -> e-way bill must be generated; goods move with a delivery challan. Management's view is wrong.

Retention of FY 2018-19 records (s.36, CGST Act):
- General rule: till the expiry of 72 months from the due date of the annual return for the year. Due date for FY 2018-19 = 31.12.2019 (extended to 31.12.2020) -> keep till 31.12.2025 (or 31.12.2026 on the extended date).
- Party to an appeal: records relating to the subject matter of the appeal must be kept for 1 year after its final disposal or the above period, whichever is later.
- The appeal is pending, so the records must be kept till 31.12.2025 / 31.12.2026 or 1 year after the appeal is finally decided, whichever is later.
questions.trap: Accepting management's 'not a supply, so no e-way bill' - rule 138 expressly covers movement for reasons other than supply.

questions.clue: 'HVB... approached the shareholders of Surgical Equipments Limited through a public announcement'

look_up.where: ICAI SM AFM - Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

questions.solve: List the defence tactics with a line of explanation each and fit them to the HVB bid; add the regulatory check on HVB's creeping stake.
questions.answer:
Measures to defend against HVB's hostile bid:
1. Divestiture - spin off some businesses into a separate subsidiary so the company becomes less attractive to HVB.
2. Crown jewels - sell or hive off the most valuable assets or divisions HVB is really after (not allowed in some countries once a bid is known).
3. Poison pill - make the company unattractive, e.g., issue convertible debentures to existing shareholders that convert when a takeover threat arises, diluting HVB's voting power.
4. Poison put - issue bonds that holders can encash at a premium on a takeover; the cash drain deters the bidder.
5. Greenmail - buy back HVB's shares at a premium in return for dropping the bid.
6. White knight - invite a friendly acquirer to buy the company on better terms and keep management.
7. White squire - sell a significant block to a friendly party with no intention to take over, blocking HVB's control.
8. Golden parachutes - large compensation to managers ousted after a takeover, raising HVB's cost.
9. Pac-man defence - make a counter-bid for HVB itself, forcing it to defend and withdraw.
Case-specific: HVB has built stakes through many non-individual shareholders - if the company is listed, check whether HVB crossed SEBI takeover-code disclosure or open-offer thresholds without complying; any breach is a legal defence.
